\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Full-replacement vs.\ accumulation.}
All experiments use full-replacement recursive chains, where each depth fully replaces the prior training corpus.
Real-world contamination typically involves accumulation, where synthetic and human data co-exist at unknown proportions \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate}.
Pilot accumulation experiments show 14--15\,pp attenuation relative to full-replacement; our results therefore represent an upper bound on feature separability, and extending the framework to accumulation settings is a priority for future work.

\paragraph{Scale and generalization boundaries.}
The primary benchmark uses 1--1.5B parameter models with controlled LoRA fine-tuning.
At 14B, cross-reference accuracy drops to 44.1\% with $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$ (nucleus/temperature); reference-model choice accounts for ${\sim}$7\,pp of the apparent degradation, and the remaining signal attenuation constitutes a scale-dependent boundary for the current feature set.
Cross-strategy transfer drops d1--d3 accuracy to 45.9\%, and on web-crawl data (C4) false positive rates reach 22\%; these gaps narrow with confidence thresholding and strategy-aware pipelines but are not fully resolved.
Additional caveats (reference model dependency, ${\leq}$11\,pp; single LoRA seed, ${\sim}$1--3\,pp uncertainty; adversarial robustness; passage length sensitivity) are detailed in the Appendix.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
This research used AI coding assistants for experiment implementation and writing drafts.
All scientific decisions, experimental design, and result interpretation were conducted by the authors.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Full-replacement vs.\ accumulation.}
All experiments use full-replacement recursive chains, where each depth fully replaces the prior training corpus.
Real-world contamination typically involves accumulation, where synthetic and human data co-exist at unknown proportions \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate}.
Pilot accumulation experiments show 14--15\,pp attenuation relative to full-replacement; our results therefore represent an upper bound on feature separability, and extending the framework to accumulation settings is a priority for future work.

\paragraph{Scale and generalization boundaries.}
The primary benchmark uses 1--1.5B parameter models with controlled LoRA fine-tuning.
At 14B, cross-reference accuracy drops to 44.1\% with $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$ (nucleus/temperature); reference-model choice accounts for ${\sim}$7\,pp of the apparent degradation, and the remaining signal attenuation constitutes a scale-dependent boundary for the current feature set.
Cross-strategy transfer drops d1--d3 accuracy to 45.9\%, and on web-crawl data (C4) false positive rates reach 22\%; these gaps narrow with confidence thresholding and strategy-aware pipelines but are not fully resolved.

文中定义 EDD 是 longest contiguous discriminable prefix，若深度集是 $D=\{0,\dots,K\}$，最大可观测 EDD 只能到最后一个测过的深度。

> All AUC profiles ... decay monotonically ... the sole non-monotonic case ... yields EDD=0

\begin{abstract}
As language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises, yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a 180K-passage benchmark spanning three model families, three decoding strategies, and four depths under controlled full-replacement chains at the 1--1.5B parameter scale.
A lightweight pipeline (19 statistical features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, classified by Random Forest) achieves d1--d3 balanced accuracy of 59--82\% across nine model--strategy cells, with the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}$) reaching 4 for all three families.
Three findings emerge: (1)~depth signal concentrates in perplexity distribution tail statistics, confirmed by classifier convergence and independent cross-perplexity features (Binoculars, 78.1\% vs.\ 78.4\%); (2)~decoding strategy affects cross-condition transfer more than model architecture (d1--d3: 45.9\% cross-strategy vs.\ 55.4\% cross-model), suggesting structurally distinct degradation trajectories; (3)~signal attenuates with scale: at 14B, accuracy drops to ${\sim}44$\% under cross-reference ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$), with reference-model choice accounting for ${\sim}7$\,pp of the apparent degradation; depth estimation claims hold most strongly within-strategy or when the decoding configuration is known.
Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines (29--33\%) confirm that binary detection scores lack ordinal depth resolution.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
In this work, we focus on the 1--1.5B parameter regime under \emph{controlled full-replacement chains}, where each generation fully replaces the prior training set, isolating the depth variable. Real-world contamination typically involves partial mixing (accumulation), where synthetic and human data co-exist at unknown proportions; the full-replacement setting provides an upper bound on depth signal strength, and we discuss implications for accumulation settings in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, the perplexity tail feature family (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{p75\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) and surprisal variance emerge as dominant depth indicators, with group-level dominance robust across all 9 model--strategy configurations and three importance measures.
The sole 8B instruction-tuned model tested (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) exhibits monotonically decreasing AUC, in contrast to the non-monotonic trajectory of its base-model counterpart; whether this regularization effect generalizes across architectures remains open (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_full}).

Following the tradition of benchmark-driven empirical studies in NLP, our contribution centers on task formalization and systematic empirical characterization rather than algorithmic novelty; the convergence of multiple classifiers (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM within 0.4\,pp; \S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) confirms that discriminative signal resides in feature design, not classifier architecture.
We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and find that a lightweight pipeline suffices: compute 19 reference-model statistical features (effective dimensionality ${\approx}$4--5 due to multicollinearity; \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) and classify with a Random Forest into $K{+}1$ depth classes.
To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K samples).
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and metric.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark ($3$ model families $\times$ $3$ decoding strategies $\times$ $4$ depths).

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} The perplexity tail feature family dominates depth discrimination across all 9 cells; $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}4$ for all three families, validated by 5-class extension (71--80\%); feature group ablation confirms perplexity tail dominance (76.6\% alone vs.\ 78.4\% full set).

    \item \textbf{Systematic characterization.} Cross-model transfer 66.4\% (d1--d3: 55.4\%), cross-domain arXiv 74.1\%, preliminary 14B 44.1\% cross-reference ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$). We identify cross-strategy transfer (d1--d3: 45.9\%) as a boundary condition: decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories, with strategy affecting transfer more than model architecture.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first \cite{shumailov2024_nature}: tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in depth $k$.
This tail erosion predicts the perplexity tail feature family as a depth marker, confirmed by its dominance across all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}).
Surprisal variance captures complementary distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
Tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below classifier resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay approaching a fixed point \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
5-class extensions to d4 (71--80\%, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm depth~4 discriminability; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics, placing a physical ceiling on EDD.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
Larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step ($\alpha$ closer to 1), so EDD should decrease with scale.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}).

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first \cite{shumailov2024_nature}: tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in depth $k$.
This tail erosion predicts the perplexity tail feature family as a depth marker, confirmed by its dominance across all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}).
Surprisal variance captures complementary distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
Tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below classifier resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay approaching a fixed point \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
5-class extensions to d4 (71--80\%, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm depth~4 discriminability; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics, placing a physical ceiling on EDD.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
Larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step ($\alpha$ closer to 1), so EDD should decrease with scale.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}).

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).
